name: wolf-spider

description.preschool: Wolf spiders are big brown furry spiders that run along the ground very fast. Mother wolf spiders carry their babies on their backs! They hunt insects at night and protect the garden.
description.elementary: Wolf spiders are large, fast-running spiders that do not build webs. Instead, they chase down insects on the ground — like tiny wolves hunting prey. They eat cutworms, beetles, and many other garden pests. If you look carefully at the soil at dusk you might see their eyes glow when you shine a light on them. Wolf spiders are completely harmless to people and are excellent garden hunters.
description.secondary: Lycosidae (wolf spiders) are cursorial hunters that rely on speed and acute vision rather than webs. They are the most abundant large ground-dwelling predatory arachnid at Oak Vista, foraging across the soil surface and through mulch layers. Prey: arthropod generalists including beetle larvae (cutworms, wireworms), dipteran pupae, small ground beetles, and crickets. Maternal care is exceptional among arachnids: females carry their egg sac attached to spinnerets, then carry spiderlings on the abdomen for 1–2 weeks post-hatching, improving juvenile survival rates. The large posterior median eyes (characteristic of Lycosidae) give acute nocturnal low-light vision. Population density tracks prey availability and is suppressed by broad-spectrum insecticide application and soil disturbance.
description.university: Family Lycosidae (Araneae) — the dominant cursorial predatory arachnid at Oak Vista, confirmed by April 2026 ground search. Foraging ecology: ambush-and-pursuit hybrid strategy; females with egg sacs or spiderlings shift to pure sit-and-wait to conserve energy. Vision system: four large posterior median eyes provide acute scotopic vision at 0.01 lux; two large anterior lateral eyes and four smaller eyes provide 360° coverage — superior to virtually all arthropod visual systems for nocturnal hunting. Prey spectrum: opportunistic arthropod predation governed by encounter rate and prey size (typically 50–150% of body size); in tomato bed context this includes Agrotis spp. (cutworm) larvae, dipteran pupae, and phytophagous beetle larvae. Soil disturbance interaction: rototilling destroys lycosid burrows and maternal retreats, suppressing populations for 3–6 weeks — aligns with 21-day macropore recovery tracking in the soil domain. Pesticide constraint: highly sensitive to pyrethroid surface sprays; systemic insecticides with soil persistence eliminate foraging populations within 72 hours of application.

sightingNotes: Abundant at Oak Vista — multiple adults observed during ground search at dusk, April 2026. Female with egg sac observed under flat stone at north bed margin. Nocturnal hunter; daytime refugia under stones and coarse mulch.

name: crab-spider

description.preschool: Crab spiders can walk sideways like a crab. They hide inside flowers and wait for bees and flies to come visit. Some can even change colour to match the flower they are sitting on!
description.elementary: Crab spiders sit perfectly still inside or on flowers and wait for insects to land. They can move sideways like a crab, which is how they got their name. Some species can slowly change colour from white to yellow to match the flower they are sitting on. They catch bees, flies, and butterflies that visit the flower. While they do catch some pollinators, they are overall part of a balanced garden food web and help keep insect populations in balance.
description.secondary: Thomisidae (crab spiders) are ambush predators specialised for floral hunting. Females of flower-dwelling species (especially Misumena vatia and related genera) can undergo physiological colour change between white and yellow via guanine pigment redistribution over 10–14 days, matching Asteraceae and Apiaceae flower heads. They do not build webs; prey capture relies entirely on ambush from concealment. Prey includes bees, flies, wasps, and butterflies. Crab spiders occupy a complex ecological position: as pollinators are among their prey, their net effect on pollination services depends on density. At natural densities in structurally complex gardens, their selective pressure on pollinator behaviour may actually improve pollination efficiency by driving pollinators to visit more flowers per foraging bout. Eggs are laid in leaf folds and guarded by the female.
description.university: Family Thomisidae (Araneae) — specialist floral ambush predators. At Oak Vista, documented on Asteraceae flower heads and dill umbels, April 2026. Colour-change physiology: guanine pigment sequestration in ommochrome-containing cells in the integument creates the colour change capacity in Misumena and allied genera; change rate is temperature-dependent (faster at 25°C than 15°C). Prey capture mechanism: forelegs I and II are adapted for rapid grasping — reaction time to prey contact is 30–50 ms; venom (neurotoxic, rapidly immobilising) is injected at the prey cervical region, exploiting arthropod neuroanatomy. Ecological impact modelling: at densities below 1 individual per 10 flowers, net pollinator-visit rate to the patch is not significantly reduced; above this threshold, avoidance learning by bees reduces floral visitation rate. Current Oak Vista density appears below threshold — no management intervention warranted.

sightingNotes: Observed on Asteraceae flowers and dill umbels, April 2026. Colour-change individual (cream-yellow) documented on dill flower head. Natural ambush predator — no intervention warranted.

name: orb-weaver

description.preschool: Orb weaver spiders make the beautiful round webs you see in the garden with morning dew on them. They sit in the middle and wait for flies and moths to fly into the web. The spider is the web's builder and engineer.
description.elementary: Orb weaver spiders spin the classic circular wheel-shaped webs that you often see covered in dew in the morning. The silk is incredibly strong — stronger than steel wire of the same thickness. The spider sits in the centre or hides at the edge, feeling for vibrations when an insect flies into the web. They mostly catch flying insects like moths, flies, leafhoppers, and wasps. A new web may be spun every night. Orb weavers are completely harmless and are a beautiful sign of garden health.
description.secondary: Araneidae (orb weavers) construct spiral orb webs with a supporting framework of non-sticky radial threads and a capture spiral of viscid (sticky) silk. The web intercepts flying insects along predictable flight corridors — garden arachnologists recommend placing orb weaver habitat features (tall perennial plant stems, fence wires, trellis) along the boundaries of vegetable beds to intercept incoming pest flights. Prey spectrum at Oak Vista: Diptera (fungus gnats, whitefly, midges), Lepidoptera (moth pests), Hemiptera (leafhoppers, whitefly), and Hymenoptera. Web reconstruction: most species consume their web each evening, recycling amino acids, and spin a fresh web before dawn. Silk properties: the viscid spiral is coated with hygroscopic glycoproteins that maintain adhesion at >30% relative humidity.
description.university: Family Araneidae (Araneae) — seasonal web-building predators at Oak Vista. Adult populations peak June–October (California); juveniles present from April as documented in 2026 assessment. Web architecture: the stereotyped orb web is produced by a genetically encoded behavioural programme involving 7 distinct silk gland types; the viscid spiral uses aggregate gland silk coated with glycoprotein glue droplets at spacing determined by leg geometry during web construction. Silk biomechanics: major ampullate silk (framework) has tensile strength ~1.75 GPa and extensibility to 30% strain — exceptional mechanical performance explained by the β-sheet nanocrystal/amorphous protein matrix organisation. Prey detection: substrate-borne vibration transmitted through radial threads to the spider; frequency and amplitude pattern discriminates prey from wind, debris, and rival spiders. Management implication: web placement in flight corridors at bed margins provides passive interception of incoming whitefly (Trialeurodes vaporariorum) and leafhopper (Empoasca spp.) populations.

sightingNotes: Juveniles and adults documented at Oak Vista April 2026 on trellis and fence wire at bed margins. Web placement consistent with active interception of flying pest corridor. No intervention warranted — ideal trellis positioning.
